questions.stem: This Gram-stained smear contains violet cocci in clusters and pink rods. Why do the violet cocci retain the crystal violet stain?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A polysaccharide capsule binds the crystal violet

choices.label: B
choices.text: Thick peptidoglycan cell wall retains the crystal violet-iodide complex

choices.label: C
choices.text: An outer membrane rich in lipopolysaccharide traps the dye

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mycolic acids in the cell wall resist acid-alcohol decolorization

explanation.summary: Gram-positive bacteria (here Staphylococcus, violet) have thick peptidoglycan walls that hold the crystal violet-iodide complex after decolorization. Gram-negative bacteria (here E. coli, pink) have a thin peptidoglycan layer, lose the violet dye and take up the safranin counterstain.
explanation.whyCorrect: Gram-positive bacteria (here Staphylococcus, violet) have thick peptidoglycan walls that hold the crystal violet-iodide complex after decolorization. Gram-negative bacteria (here E. coli, pink) have a thin peptidoglycan layer, lose the violet dye and take up the safranin counterstain.

questions.stem: A sputum smear stained with carbol fuchsin, washed with acid alcohol, and counterstained with methylene blue shows the red rods seen here. Which cell wall component explains their staining?

explanation.summary: This is an acid-fast (Ziehl-Neelsen) stain. Acid-fast organisms such as Mycobacteria (and Nocardia) have large amounts of mycolic acids in their cell walls that resist acid-alcohol decolorization, so they stay bright red against the blue background.
explanation.whyCorrect: This is an acid-fast (Ziehl-Neelsen) stain. Acid-fast organisms such as Mycobacteria (and Nocardia) have large amounts of mycolic acids in their cell walls that resist acid-alcohol decolorization, so they stay bright red against the blue background.

questions.stem: In this preparation the background is stained dark and each bacterium is surrounded by a clear halo. What does the clear halo represent?

explanation.summary: Capsules do not bind most dyes, so they are shown by negative staining of the background with India ink (or nigrosine). The capsule appears as a clear halo around each cell. Capsules can contribute to a bacterium's ability to cause disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: Capsules do not bind most dyes, so they are shown by negative staining of the background with India ink (or nigrosine). The capsule appears as a clear halo around each cell. Capsules can contribute to a bacterium's ability to cause disease.

questions.stem: A Gram stain shows the violet cocci arranged as shown (arrow). Which genus most typically has this appearance?

explanation.summary: Gram-positive cocci arranged in chains (short single-file lines) are characteristic of Streptococcus species. Staphylococcus forms grape-like clusters, Neisseria are gram-negative diplococci, E. coli is a gram-negative rod, and Mycobacteria are acid-fast rods.
explanation.whyCorrect: Gram-positive cocci arranged in chains (short single-file lines) are characteristic of Streptococcus species. Staphylococcus forms grape-like clusters, Neisseria are gram-negative diplococci, E. coli is a gram-negative rod, and Mycobacteria are acid-fast rods.

questions.stem: A Gram stain shows violet cocci grouped as shown (arrows). Which genus most typically has this appearance?

explanation.summary: Gram-positive cocci that bunch together like grapes (clusters) are characteristic of Staphylococcus species. Streptococci form chains, Neisseria are gram-negative diplococci, E. coli is a gram-negative rod, and Nocardia forms branching filaments.
explanation.whyCorrect: Gram-positive cocci that bunch together like grapes (clusters) are characteristic of Staphylococcus species. Streptococci form chains, Neisseria are gram-negative diplococci, E. coli is a gram-negative rod, and Nocardia forms branching filaments.

questions.stem: The diagram shows a gene flanked by mobile DNA sequences moving from a plasmid into the bacterial chromosome. Clinically, genes moved this way most often encode what?

explanation.summary: Transposons must flank both sides of a gene to move it. They let DNA jump within the genome and between plasmids and chromosomal DNA, often carrying drug-resistance genes such as beta-lactamase. Once the gene is in the chromosome, all future progeny of that bacterium carry it.
explanation.whyCorrect: Transposons must flank both sides of a gene to move it. They let DNA jump within the genome and between plasmids and chromosomal DNA, often carrying drug-resistance genes such as beta-lactamase. Once the gene is in the chromosome, all future progeny of that bacterium carry it.

questions.stem: Which horizontal gene transfer mechanism is illustrated, in which a plasmid passes from one bacterium to another through direct physical contact?

explanation.summary: In conjugation, an F+ bacterium uses the sex pilus encoded by its F plasmid to form a mating bridge with an F- cell. A single strand of the plasmid is transferred and copied, so both cells end up F+. No chromosomal DNA is transferred. Conjugation is the most common horizontal gene transfer mechanism and spreads plasmid-borne antibiotic resistance.
explanation.whyCorrect: In conjugation, an F+ bacterium uses the sex pilus encoded by its F plasmid to form a mating bridge with an F- cell. A single strand of the plasmid is transferred and copied, so both cells end up F+. No chromosomal DNA is transferred. Conjugation is the most common horizontal gene transfer mechanism and spreads plasmid-borne antibiotic resistance.

questions.stem: In this variant of conjugation the F plasmid is integrated into the donor chromosome. Compared with standard F+ x F- conjugation, what can the recipient receive?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bacteriophage DNA packaged in a capsid

choices.label: B
choices.text: A fragment of the donor's chromosomal DNA

choices.label: C
choices.text: Only a complete copy of the F plasmid

explanation.summary: In a high-frequency recombination (Hfr) strain, the F plasmid sits in the chromosome. Transfer starts at the plasmid origin and can carry flanking chromosomal DNA into the F- cell, usually only a fragment of the donor chromosome, producing a recombinant recipient. Standard F+ x F- conjugation transfers only the plasmid.
explanation.whyCorrect: In a high-frequency recombination (Hfr) strain, the F plasmid sits in the chromosome. Transfer starts at the plasmid origin and can carry flanking chromosomal DNA into the F- cell, usually only a fragment of the donor chromosome, producing a recombinant recipient. Standard F+ x F- conjugation transfers only the plasmid.

questions.topicName: Normal Flora: Role in Health and Disease
questions.stem: A woman has vaginal itching and burning. Speculum exam shows the white plaques seen here. Which organism, part of the normal flora, is the most likely cause?

explanation.summary: This is vulvovaginal candidiasis (a vaginal yeast infection). Candida species are normal vaginal and oral flora that can overgrow, for example after antibiotics kill competing bacteria. 'Albicans' means to whiten, matching the white plaques. Gardnerella overgrowth causes bacterial vaginosis instead.
explanation.whyCorrect: This is vulvovaginal candidiasis (a vaginal yeast infection). Candida species are normal vaginal and oral flora that can overgrow, for example after antibiotics kill competing bacteria. 'Albicans' means to whiten, matching the white plaques. Gardnerella overgrowth causes bacterial vaginosis instead.

questions.topicName: Normal Flora: Role in Health and Disease
questions.stem: An infant has the white plaques on the tongue and oral mucosa seen here. Which organism is responsible?

explanation.summary: This is thrush (oral candidiasis), an overgrowth of Candida in the oral cavity. It is linked to antibiotic use, birth control use, trauma, poorly fitting dentures or immunosuppression. In a patient with no obvious cause, thrush can signal a failing immune system, so check a CBC.
explanation.whyCorrect: This is thrush (oral candidiasis), an overgrowth of Candida in the oral cavity. It is linked to antibiotic use, birth control use, trauma, poorly fitting dentures or immunosuppression. In a patient with no obvious cause, thrush can signal a failing immune system, so check a CBC.

questions.topicName: Normal Flora: Role in Health and Disease
questions.stem: The cells on the right are vaginal squamous epithelial cells coated with bacteria. The bacterium most characteristically coating these cells is which organism?

explanation.summary: Bacteria-coated vaginal epithelial cells are clue cells, the finding used to diagnose bacterial vaginosis. The coating organisms are small coccobacilli, Gardnerella vaginalis. Lactobacillus is the dominant normal vaginal flora that is displaced in this condition.
explanation.whyCorrect: Bacteria-coated vaginal epithelial cells are clue cells, the finding used to diagnose bacterial vaginosis. The coating organisms are small coccobacilli, Gardnerella vaginalis. Lactobacillus is the dominant normal vaginal flora that is displaced in this condition.

questions.topicName: Normal Flora: Role in Health and Disease
questions.stem: A woman has a thin, grayish vaginal discharge with a fishy odor and little inflammation. A smear shows the large epithelial cells covered in small purple coccobacilli seen here. What is the diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Epithelial cells coated with Gardnerella vaginalis coccobacilli are clue cells, the diagnostic finding of bacterial vaginosis. BV causes a thin gray-white discharge with a fishy smell from released amines and typically less burning, itching and inflammation than vulvovaginal candidiasis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Epithelial cells coated with Gardnerella vaginalis coccobacilli are clue cells, the diagnostic finding of bacterial vaginosis. BV causes a thin gray-white discharge with a fishy smell from released amines and typically less burning, itching and inflammation than vulvovaginal candidiasis.

questions.topicName: Normal Flora: Role in Health and Disease
questions.stem: The anatomic difference shown between a young child and an adult is a major risk factor for which childhood infection?

explanation.summary: In children the Eustachian tube is shorter, narrower and more horizontal than in adults. This is a major anatomic risk factor for acute otitis media, letting nasopharyngeal flora reach the middle ear.
explanation.whyCorrect: In children the Eustachian tube is shorter, narrower and more horizontal than in adults. This is a major anatomic risk factor for acute otitis media, letting nasopharyngeal flora reach the middle ear.

questions.topicName: Normal Flora: Role in Health and Disease
questions.stem: The right-hand image shows a red, bulging tympanic membrane in a febrile child with ear pain. The three most common bacterial causes of this condition are which group?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Staphylococcus aureus, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Escherichia coli

choices.label: B
choices.text: Staphylococcus epidermidis, Corynebacterium species, Cutibacterium acnes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Streptococcus pyogenes, Neisseria meningitidis, Listeria monocytogenes

explanation.summary: This is acute otitis media: an inflamed, bulging eardrum with pus behind it, plus pain and fever. Its three most common bacterial causes are S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae and M. catarrhalis, all normal flora of the nasopharynx.
explanation.whyCorrect: This is acute otitis media: an inflamed, bulging eardrum with pus behind it, plus pain and fever. Its three most common bacterial causes are S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae and M. catarrhalis, all normal flora of the nasopharynx.

questions.topicName: Normal Flora: Role in Health and Disease
questions.stem: A 4-month-old infant has fever, a petechial rash and necrosis of the hands and feet, as shown. Which encapsulated organism is classically responsible?

explanation.summary: The lecture shows this image as a 4-month-old with necrosis of the hands and feet due to N. meningitidis. Along with S. pneumoniae and H. influenzae, it is one of the most common causes of serious bacterial infection in children and can be carried as nasopharyngeal flora.
explanation.whyCorrect: The lecture shows this image as a 4-month-old with necrosis of the hands and feet due to N. meningitidis. Along with S. pneumoniae and H. influenzae, it is one of the most common causes of serious bacterial infection in children and can be carried as nasopharyngeal flora.

questions.topicName: Normal Flora: Role in Health and Disease
questions.stem: This infant developed the hemorrhagic, necrotic skin lesions shown from a severe Neisseria meningitidis infection at about 4 months of age. Why are infants especially vulnerable at this age?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The infant's normal flora has not yet colonized the nasopharynx

choices.label: B
choices.text: Maternal transplacental IgG has waned before the infant makes adequate antibodies of its own

choices.label: C
choices.text: Breast milk IgA promotes bacterial adherence

choices.label: D
choices.text: Infants lack a complement system until 1 year of age

explanation.summary: Transplacental maternal IgG gives early protection but declines over the first months. Until the infant makes enough antibody of its own, exposure to S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae or N. meningitidis can cause severe infection. This is why Hib and pneumococcal vaccines start at 2 months.
explanation.whyCorrect: Transplacental maternal IgG gives early protection but declines over the first months. Until the infant makes enough antibody of its own, exposure to S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae or N. meningitidis can cause severe infection. This is why Hib and pneumococcal vaccines start at 2 months.

questions.topicName: Normal Flora: Role in Health and Disease
questions.stem: This necrotic foot belongs to an infant with an invasive Neisseria meningitidis infection. In carriers, this organism typically lives as normal flora at which site?

explanation.summary: S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae and N. meningitidis can be carried as normal flora of the nasopharynx. Encapsulated strains are much more likely to cause invasive disease, such as the meningococcal infection that caused this limb necrosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae and N. meningitidis can be carried as normal flora of the nasopharynx. Encapsulated strains are much more likely to cause invasive disease, such as the meningococcal infection that caused this limb necrosis.

questions.topicName: Normal Flora: Role in Health and Disease
questions.stem: A patient on antibiotics develops severe watery diarrhea and cramping. The colon shows the yellow-white plaques seen here. Which organism is responsible?

explanation.summary: Yellow-white pseudomembranes indicate pseudomembranous colitis from C. difficile, a member of normal lower-GI flora. Antibiotics kill competing flora and let C. difficile overgrow and release toxins. Recurrence is common (20-60%), and fecal transplant can restore normal flora.
explanation.whyCorrect: Yellow-white pseudomembranes indicate pseudomembranous colitis from C. difficile, a member of normal lower-GI flora. Antibiotics kill competing flora and let C. difficile overgrow and release toxins. Recurrence is common (20-60%), and fecal transplant can restore normal flora.
